title: Man. Post. Cap. VII: PLAC — temporal vs eternal; likeness fails for all posterity
pass_a_gloss: Placeus: if that was his opponent's mind, he should have said so plainly—Placeus is no Oedipus. The example fails (1) because it concerns only temporal penalty, while Adam's sin is imputed to eternal death and to a penalty that is itself sin and necessitates further sin—the main clash with a judge's and the law's justice; (2) many on the other side disapprove father-to-child or grandson imputation as well as approve it (pp. 81–83 and more if he wished); (3) nothing like an imputation ranging even now after millennia over all posterity without exception; (4) such examples come from wrath or necessity of guarding princes' lives and the republic's safety—neither applies in the matter at hand. Immediate imputation of Adam's sin does not curb sinning but strips the habit of doing well or obeying and subjects men to necessity of sinning, against the end of the law and of vindicating justice.
pass_b_english: PLAC. If that was the mind of him with whom I had to do, it would have been fair that he hint it more openly: for I am no Oedipus. Be that as it may, besides what I have so far noted, two or three things stand in the way of this example's being fitted to that end. First: in that example only a temporal penalty is in view, whereas Adam's sin is said to be imputed unto eternal death—and not to that alone, but also to a penalty that is itself sin, and sets a man in a state where he cannot thereafter not sin. That is what seems to us chiefly to clash with a judge's and the law's justice. Next: if some men have approved imputing a father's crime to children or grandsons, there have not been wanting on the other side—and perhaps far more—who disapproved. The learned man himself mentions some on pp. 81–83; he could have mentioned many more if he wished. So the likeness does not heal the scandal, except perhaps in some part. Further, what like thing can be brought for an imputation that even now, after some thousands of years, ranges over all posterity, none excepted? Finally, such examples either wrath extorted, or the necessity of guarding princes' lives and the republic's safety—neither of which has place in the matter at hand. Indeed, so far is that immediate imputation of Adam's sin from keeping men from sinning that, on the contrary, they are stripped of the habit of doing well or obeying, and subjected to a necessity of sinning—which seems violently to abhor from the end of the law and of vindicating justice.
source_text: PLAC. Si haec eius mens fuit quicum mihi res erat, aequum fuisset, ut eam innueret apertius: non enim sum Oedipus. Quicquid sit, praeter ea quae hactenus a me sunt observata, quominus ad id accommodatum sit hoc exemplum duo vel tria obstant, illud primo, quod in eo exemplo non agitur nisi de poena temporali, cum imputari dicatur peccatum Adae ad mortem aeternam, nec ad eam tantum, sed etiam ad poenam quae sit peccatum, & hominem in eo statu constituat, ut non possit deinceps non peccare. Hoc enim est quod potissimum repugnare judicis & legis justitiae nobis videtur. Deinde, si quidam ex hominibus criminis paterni imputationem liberis aut nepotibus approbaverunt, non defuerunt ex altera parte, & fortasse multo plures qui improbaverunt: Commemorat nonnullos ipse vir doctus pag. 81. 82. 83. potuisset multo plures si voluisset. Itaque non medetur scandalo similitudo nisi forte ex aliqua parte. Praeterea, quid simile afferri potest eiusmodi imputationi, quae etiamnum post aliquot annorum millia grassatur in omnes posteros, nemine quidem excepto? Denique eiusmodi exempla vel ira extorsit, vel necessitas tuendae vitae principum & salutis reipublicae: quorum neutrum in re de qua agitur locum habet. Imo tantum abest ut imputatione illa immediata peccati Adami homines a peccando inhibeantur, ut contra priventur bene agendi seu obediendi habitu, & subijciantur necessitati peccandi: id quod a fine legis & justitiae vindicis vehementer abhorrere videtur.
